text:
For never is hatred
laid to rest by hate,
it’s laid to rest by love:
this is an ancient teaching.
note: Anger and grudges; answering hurt with love
Conflict with people who do not understand

text:
By hard work and diligence,
by restraint and by self-control,
a smart person would build an island
that the floods cannot overflow.
note: Building steadiness against overwhelm

text:
The mind quivers and quakes,
hard to guard, hard to curb.
The discerning straighten it out,
like a fletcher an arrow.
note: A restless, anxious mind

text:
A wrongly directed mind
would do you more harm
than a hater to the hated,
or an enemy to their foe.
note: Self-destructive thinking and rumination

text:
Don’t find fault with others,
with what they’ve done or left undone.
You should only watch yourself,
what you’ve done or left undone.
note: Judging others; turning attention to oneself

text:
“Sons are mine, wealth is mine”—
thus the fool frets.
For even your self is not your own,
let alone your sons or wealth.
note: Possessiveness, worry over family and money

text:
The fool who thinks they’re a fool
is wise at least to that extent.
But the true fool is said to be one
who imagines that they are wise.
note: Humility, mistakes, overconfidence

text:
It’s not good to do a deed
that plagues you later on,
for which you weep and wail,
as its effect stays with you.
note: Regret and guilt over something done

text:
Regard one who sees your faults
as a guide to a hidden treasure.
Stay close to one so intelligent and astute
who curbs you when you need it.
Sticking close to such an impartial person,
things get better, not worse.
note: Receiving criticism and honest feedback

text:
As the wind cannot stir
a solid mass of rock,
so too blame and praise
do not affect the wise.
note: Criticism, praise, and staying steady

text:
True persons give up everything,
they don’t cajole for the things they desire.
Though touched by sadness or happiness,
the astute appear neither depressed nor elated.
note: Emotional balance in sorrow and joy

text:
Better than a thousand
meaningless sayings
is a single meaningful saying,
hearing which brings you peace.
note: Noise and overload; one meaningful word brings peace

text:
The supreme conqueror is
not he who conquers a million men in battle,
but he who conquers a single man:
himself.
note: Self-mastery, struggle with oneself

text:
If you do something good,
do it again and again,
set your heart on it,
for piling up goodness is joyful.
note: Building good habits; discouragement about progress

text:
Think not lightly of goodness,
that it won’t come back to you.
The pot is filled with water
falling drop by drop;
the attentive one is filled with goodness
piled up bit by bit.
note: Small steady efforts add up over time

text:
Don’t speak harshly,
they may speak harshly back.
For aggressive speech is painful,
and the rod may spring back on you.
note: Anger and harsh words in conflict

text:
Fancy chariots of kings wear out,
and even this body gets old.
But the truth of the good never gets old—
so the good proclaim to the good.
note: Ageing and what lasts

text:
If you knew your self as beloved,
you’d look after it so well.
In one of the night’s three watches,
an astute person would remain alert.
note: Self-care and treating yourself as worth caring for

text:
One is indeed the lord of oneself,
for who else would be one’s lord?
By means of a well-tamed self,
one gains a lord that’s rare indeed.
note: Self-mastery and taking responsibility for oneself

text:
It’s easy to do bad things
harmful to oneself,
but good things that are helpful
are the hardest things to do.
note: Struggling to do what is good for you

text:
For it is by oneself that evil’s done,
one is corrupted by oneself.
It’s by oneself that evil’s not done,
one is purified by oneself.
Purity and impurity are personal matters,
no one can purify another.
note: Guilt and personal responsibility for change

text:
Let us live so very happily,
loving among the hostile.
Among hostile humans,
let us live with love.
note: Staying kind among hostile people

text:
Let us live so very happily,
content among the greedy.
Among greedy humans,
let us live content.
note: Contentment amid envy and ambition around you

text:
Victory breeds enmity;
the defeated sleep badly.
The peaceful sleep at ease,
having left victory and defeat behind.
note: Rivalry, winning and losing, and restlessness

text:
Sorrow springs from what we hold dear,
fear springs from what we hold dear;
one free from holding anything dear
has no sorrow, let alone fear.
note: Grief and fear rooted in loving and losing

text:
Sorrow springs from desire,
fear springs from desire;
one free from desire
has no sorrow, let alone fear.
note: Sorrow and fear rooted in wanting

text:
When anger surges like a lurching chariot,
keep it in check.
That’s what I call a charioteer;
others just hold the reins.
note: Anger rising and needing restraint

text:
Defeat anger with kindness,
villainy with virtue,
stinginess with giving,
and lies with truth.
note: Answering anger and wrongdoing with goodness

text:
It’s always been this way, Atula,
it’s not just today.
They blame you when you’re silent,
they blame you when you speak a lot,
and even when you speak just right:
no one in the world escapes blame.
note: Being criticised whatever you do

text:
There is no fire like greed,
no crime like hate,
no net like delusion,
no river like craving.
note: The destructive pull of greed and hate

text:
It’s easy to see the faults of others,
hard to see one’s own.
For the faults of others
are tossed high like hay,
while one’s own are hidden,
as a cheat hides a bad hand.
note: Blindness to our own faults
Ageing without growing wiser

text:
From meditation springs wisdom,
without meditation, wisdom ends.
Knowing these two paths—
of progress and decline—
you should conduct yourself
so that wisdom grows.
note: Practice as the source of wisdom

text:
A bad deed is better left undone,
for it will plague you later on.
A good deed is better done,
one that does not plague you.
note: Guilt and choosing what you will not regret

text:
In the past my mind wandered
how it wished, where it liked, as it pleased.
Now I’ll carefully guide it,
as a trainer with a hook guides a rutting elephant.
note: A restless, wandering mind and learning to steer it.

text:
Delight in diligence!
Take good care of your mind!
Pull yourself out of this pit,
like an elephant sunk in a bog.
note: Feeling stuck in a low place; caring for your mind.

text:
It’s better to wander alone,
there’s no fellowship with fools.
Wander alone and do no wrong,
at ease like a tusker in the wilds.
note: Loneliness and choosing solitude over poor company.
Gratitude for friends, contentment, and a life well lived.

text:
Whoever is beaten by this wretched craving,
this attachment to the world,
their sorrow grows,
like grass in the rain.

But whoever prevails over this wretched craving,
so hard to get over in the world,
their sorrows fall from them,
like a drop from a lotus-leaf.
note: Craving and attachment feeding sorrow; relief when it loosens.

text:
A tree grows back even when cut down,
so long as its roots are strong and undamaged;
suffering springs up again and again,
so long as the tendency to craving is not pulled out.
note: Pain that keeps returning because its root remains.

text:
Self is indeed the lord of self,
for who else would be one’s lord?
Self is indeed the home of self,
so restrain yourself,
as a merchant his thoroughbred steed.
note: Taking responsibility for yourself; being your own home.

text:
Why the matted hair, you simpleton,
and why the skin of deer?
The tangle is inside you,
yet you polish up your outsides.
note: Polishing appearances while the inner tangle remains.

display: Lectures (Complete Works, Vol. II): Work And Its Secret
text: If we examine our own lives, we find that the greatest cause of sorrow is this: we take up something, and put our whole energy on it — perhaps it is a failure and yet we cannot give it up. We know that it is hurting us, that any further clinging to it is simply bringing misery on us; still, we cannot tear ourselves away from it. The bee came to sip the honey, but its feet stuck to the honey-pot and it could not get away.
note: Clinging to something that is hurting you and cannot let go

display: Lectures (Complete Works, Vol. II): Work And Its Secret
text: There are men who are never attracted by anything. They can never love, they are hard-hearted and apathetic; they escape most of the miseries of life. But the wall never feels misery, the wall never loves, is never hurt; but it is the wall, after all. Surely it is better to be attached and caught, than to be a wall. Therefore the man who never loves, who is hard and stony, escaping most of the miseries of life, escapes also its joys. We do not want that. That is weakness, that is death. That soul has not been awakened that never feels weakness, never feels misery. That is a callous state. We do not want that.
note: Fear of being hurt by love; numbness versus feeling

display: Lectures (Complete Works, Vol. II): Work And Its Secret
text: We get caught. How? Not by what we give, but by what we expect. We get misery in return for our love; not from the fact that we love, but from the fact that we want love in return. There is no misery where there is no want. Desire, want, is the father of all misery. Desires are bound by the laws of success and failure. Desires must bring misery.
note: Hurt from loving and expecting love in return

display: Lectures (Complete Works, Vol. II): Work And Its Secret
text: Every day we renew our determination to be unattached. We cast our eyes back and look at the past objects of our love and attachment, and feel how every one of them made us miserable. We went down into the depths of despondency because of our “love”! We found ourselves mere slaves in the hands of others, we were dragged down and down! And we make a fresh determination: “Henceforth, I will be master of myself; henceforth, I will have control over myself.” But the time comes, and the same story once more! Again the soul is caught and cannot get out. The bird is in a net, struggling and fluttering. This is our life.
note: Repeating the same painful attachments despite resolutions

display: Lectures (Complete Works, Vol. II): Work And Its Secret
text: We are all the time, from our childhood, trying to lay the blame upon something outside ourselves. We are always standing up to set right other people, and not ourselves. If we are miserable, we say, “Oh, the world is a devil’s world.” We curse others and say, “What infatuated fools!” But why should we be in such a world, if we really are so good? If this is a devil’s world, we must be devils also; why else should we be here? “Oh, the people of the world are so selfish!” True enough; but why should we be found in that company, if we be better? Just think of that.
note: Blaming others and the world for our unhappiness

display: Lectures (Complete Works, Vol. II): Work And Its Secret
text: We are to take care of ourselves — that much we can do — and give up attending to others for a time. Let us perfect the means; the end will take care of itself. For the world can be good and pure, only if our lives are good and pure. It is an effect, and we are the means. Therefore, let us purify ourselves. Let us make ourselves perfect.
note: Changing the world by first working on yourself
